university: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center

documents.unit: Chief Information Officer / AI Governance and Risk Committee
documents.title: HSC OP 52.21, Acceptable Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools
documents.summary: An institution-wide operating policy on acceptable AI use covering education, research, clinical and administrative work. It is mostly about data governance, disclosure, verification and a governing committee; its only coursework content is that academic work with AI must follow what the instructor allows.
documents.stance_why: The document sets principles and data rules for all users but never bans or permits AI in coursework itself; the only academic-work rule is that AI should not be used for 'completion of academic work in a manner not allowed by the instructor', which hands the decision to instructors.

units.why: The Purpose section states why the policy exists: 'responsible, ethical, and compliant use' of AI across education, research, clinical care and administration, which makes it an institution-wide framework (P56) rather than a coursework rule.
units.anchor: establish clear expectations and guidelines for the responsible, ethical, and compliant use of artificial intelligence
units.frag_end: academic, clinical, research and business operations.

units.why: The Review clause fixes a schedule: the OP 'will be reviewed by March 1 of each odd-numbered year', so it is a review cycle (P54), not a rule on AI use.
units.anchor: reviewed by March 1 of each odd-numbered year

units.why: The same Review sentence names the CIO and Chief Compliance Officer as reviewers and the AI Governance and Risk Committee for substantive revisions, so it also says who owns the policy (P80). P54 captures the cycle; this unit captures ownership.
units.anchor: by the Chief Information Officer and the Chief Compliance Officer
units.policy: The Chief Information Officer and the Chief Compliance Officer review the OP, with substantive revisions forwarded to the AI Governance and Risk Committee and People and Operations Council.

units.why: The definition says AI tools 'use machine learning (ML), natural language processing, large language models, computer vision', which sets the policy's scope; this is a definition (P61).
units.anchor: software, systems, or applications that use machine learning (ML), natural language processing, large language models

units.why: The exclusions list ('basic rule-based spell/grammar checkers', calculators) says routine non-AI utilities fall outside the policy; this fits P100 (exempt routine features) partly, because the exemption is a scope definition and is conditional on no AI/ML features.
units.anchor: Basic deterministic utilities (e.g., calculators, basic rule-based spell/grammar checkers
units.policy: Basic deterministic utilities such as calculators, basic rule-based spell/grammar checkers, simple macros and mail-merge are not AI tools under this policy unless they incorporate AI/ML features.
units.fit_note: Exclusion is a scope definition for non-AI utilities, not an exemption of AI features from a restrictive rule.

units.why: The boundary rule says features marketed as 'AI,' 'smart,' 'assist,' 'predictive' are in scope 'even if the larger product would otherwise be excluded', which covers AI built into other products (P07) and sets scope.
units.anchor: those capabilities are in scope even if the larger product would otherwise be excluded
units.frag_start: If a product or feature advertises
units.fit_note: Concerns AI embedded in general software and vendor updates, not editors or IDEs specifically.

units.why: 'When in doubt, treat the feature as an AI tool' and consult the committee; users resolve uncertainty by asking, matching P10, though the addressee is a committee, not an instructor.
units.anchor: When in doubt, treat the feature as an AI tool
units.fit_note: Users ask the AI Governance and Risk Committee for a determination, not an instructor, and the default is to treat the feature as AI.

units.why: The opening sentence of Policy/Procedure says 'it's essential to use these technologies responsibly', a general principle with no specific rule; it frames the institution-wide framework (P56).
units.anchor: it's essential to use these technologies responsibly

units.why: Principle 1a says 'AI use must be disclosed and documented appropriately', a binding duty to disclose; P24 is the nearest type though this is a general principle, not a per-submission rule.
units.anchor: AI use must be disclosed and documented appropriately.
units.frag_end: produced or significantly influenced by AI.

units.why: Principle 1a continues 'Documentation should include the type of AI tool used, its purpose, and any limitations', specifying what to record about the tool; this is P25.
units.anchor: Documentation should include the type of AI tool used, its purpose, and any limitations
units.fit_note: Asks for tool type, purpose and limitations, not the exact prompt or output.

units.why: Principle 1b: 'Human users have final responsibility for all decisions and outcomes resulting from AI use', i.e. users own what they do with AI (P29).
units.anchor: Human users have final responsibility for all decisions and outcomes resulting from AI use.

units.why: 'Users must evaluate AI outputs, recognize the tool's limitations, and take corrective action' requires verifying and critically evaluating AI output (P31).
units.anchor: Users must evaluate AI outputs, recognize the tool’s limitations, and take corrective action

units.why: 'Accountability also involves documenting decisions made with AI tools to maintain traceability' is a record-keeping duty; closest to P26 (keep logs) but it concerns decisions, not student transcripts.
units.anchor: documenting decisions made with AI tools to maintain traceability
units.fit_note: Documents decisions made with AI for traceability, not chat logs or reflections submitted with work.

units.why: Principle 1c says AI 'must be used in ways that uphold fair treatment of all individuals and avoid discrimination', naming bias and harms (P53).
units.anchor: AI tools must be used in ways that uphold fair treatment of all individuals and

units.why: Users must identify and mitigate 'unfair or harmful impacts' and review 'training data, models, and applications' to avoid reinforcing disparities; a bias-mitigation duty (P53).
units.anchor: Users are responsible for identifying, assessing, and mitigating instances where AI outputs may lead to

units.why: Principle 1d: 'AI use must protect sensitive, confidential, and personally identifiable information' is a data-protection rule (P50).
units.anchor: AI use must protect sensitive, confidential, and personally identifiable information.

units.why: 'Data input into AI systems should be minimized to only what is necessary for the task' is a data-minimization rule, part of protecting personal data (P50).
units.anchor: Data input into AI systems should be minimized to only what is necessary

units.why: Principle 1e: 'AI is intended as a decision-support tool, not a replacement for human judgment'; AI must not replace human decisions (P73), with no student-learning content so P32 does not fit.
units.anchor: AI is intended as a decision-support tool, not a replacement for human judgment.
units.fit_note: General human-judgment principle not limited to decisions about individuals.

units.why: 'All outputs must be subject to human review, with the capacity to override or modify' sets human review of AI output as a requirement (P73 nearest).
units.anchor: All outputs must be subject to human review, with the capacity to override or modify
units.fit_note: Human review of all AI outputs, broader than consequential decisions about people.

units.why: 'continuous monitoring of AI performance to ensure it aligns with institutional values' calls for ongoing monitoring of deployed AI (P98).
units.anchor: Supervision also includes continuous monitoring of AI performance

units.why: The AI Governance and Risk Committee 'is established by the President's Cabinet to provide strategic and operational oversight', naming the body that governs the policy (P80).
units.anchor: provide strategic and operational oversight for all AI-related activities
units.policy: The AI Governance and Risk Committee, established by the President's Cabinet, provides strategic and operational oversight for all AI-related activities.

units.why: The committee membership list (Chief Compliance Officer, CIO, Provost or Academic Affairs representative, optional faculty and student representatives) says who sits on the governing body, which describes how governance is composed (P80).
units.anchor: Faculty and Student Representatives (optional)
units.policy: Faculty and student representatives may sit on the AI Governance and Risk Committee as optional members.

units.why: The committee must 'Approve and maintain AI policies, procedures, and standards', assigning policy ownership (P80).
units.anchor: Approve and maintain AI policies, procedures, and standards.

units.why: The committee must 'Review and approve proposed AI tools and high-risk projects' across education among other domains, which is tool approval (P65).
units.anchor: Review and approve proposed AI tools and high-risk projects
units.frag_end: clinical, research, education, and administrative domains.

units.why: The committee must 'Assess risk, including privacy, security, bias, and ethical considerations'; risk assessment of AI tools is part of institutional review (P65).
units.anchor: Assess risk, including privacy, security, bias, and ethical considerations.

units.why: The committee must 'Monitor AI system performance and compliance post-deployment', which is monitoring of deployed systems (P98).
units.anchor: Monitor AI system performance and compliance post-deployment.

units.why: The committee must 'Evaluate vendor partnerships and contracts for AI solutions', matching P65 on review of AI contracts and vendors.
units.anchor: Evaluate vendor partnerships and contracts for AI solutions.

units.why: The committee must 'Oversee training programs and competency requirements for AI users', which provides for AI training (P70).
units.anchor: Oversee training programs and competency requirements for AI users.

units.why: The committee must 'Receive and review reports of incidents or concerns', a channel for reporting AI problems (P71).
units.anchor: Receive and review reports of incidents or concerns; recommend mitigation and corrective actions.

units.why: Allowable Use ties AI use to the four data classes in OP 56.04; users follow existing data-classification rules, so this is a compliance-with-existing-policy rule (P77).
units.anchor: all TTUHSC-owned data is classified into four types
units.frag_end: privacy, security, legal, and ethical considerations.

units.why: 'Public Data may be used freely with AI tools' permits AI use with public data; this fits P50 partly, as the rule about what data may go into AI.
units.anchor: Public Data may be used freely with AI tools
units.policy: Public Data may be used freely with AI tools for generating insights, summaries, or training, unless the platform restricts it.
units.fit_note: Permission for public data to be used freely, not a protection rule.

units.why: Sensitive, Controlled and Regulated Data may be used only with tools 'managed by TTUHSC and covered by contracts explicitly protecting TTUHSC data'; a rule to prefer vetted tools and protect data (P50).
units.anchor: tools that are managed by TTUHSC and covered by contracts explicitly protecting TTUHSC data
units.policy: Sensitive, Controlled, and Regulated Data can be used with AI tools that are managed by TTUHSC and covered by contracts explicitly protecting TTUHSC data, ensuring the data is not used for training models or is isolated in a separate instance inaccessible to external parties.

units.why: 'AI tools should be used as decision-support tools and not as decision-making tools' repeats the human-judgment principle in the use section; it keeps humans responsible for decisions (P73).
units.anchor: AI tools should be used as decision-support tools and not as decision- making tools.
units.fit_note: General decision-support rule, not limited to decisions about individuals.

units.why: 'In all cases, use should be consistent with the HSC OP 52.09... and HSC OP 56.01' ties AI use to existing university policies (P77).
units.anchor: use should be consistent with the
units.frag_end: Acceptable Use of Information Technology Resources

units.why: 'Users may use only the information and information systems to which they have been given authorized access' limits data access in AI use; a confidentiality and compliance duty (P50).
units.anchor: Users may use only the information and information systems to which they have been given

units.why: Anyone with access 'will take reasonable and necessary steps to maintain the confidentiality and privacy' of employee, student and patient information, a data-protection duty (P50).
units.anchor: will take reasonable and necessary steps to maintain the confidentiality and privacy
units.frag_end: made confidential by TTUHSC policies or law

units.why: Prohibited Use 4a: AI tools 'that lack a TTUHSC contract and appropriate data-sharing safeguards are not approved' for sensitive data; use of unvetted tools is barred (P50).
units.anchor: AI tools that lack a TTUHSC contract and appropriate data- sharing safeguards are not approved

units.why: 4b: 'AI tools may not be used with personal, confidential, proprietary, or other sensitive information' without a protecting contract; it names FERPA student records and HIPAA data (P50).
units.anchor: AI tools may not be used with personal, confidential, proprietary, or other sensitive information

units.why: 4c says AI 'should not be used to generate outputs that would be considered non-public', such as proprietary or unpublished research and legal analysis; this fits P62 (research) partly.
units.anchor: AI tools should not be used to generate outputs that would be considered non-public.
units.fit_note: Covers non-public outputs in general, including research and legal analysis, not only research and scholarship.

units.why: The examples in 4c include 'completion of academic work in a manner not allowed by the instructor', so students may not use AI for academic work beyond what the instructor allows; the instructor sets the rule (P04), and I chose P04 over P19 because the unit defers to the instructor rather than itself banning AI-produced work.
units.anchor: completion of academic work in a manner not allowed by the instructor
units.frag_end: creation of non-public instructional materials; and grading.
units.policy: AI tools should not be used to generate non-public outputs, including completion of academic work in a manner not allowed by the instructor.
units.fit_note: Instructor discretion is implicit; the rule bans only AI use the instructor has not allowed.

units.why: The 4c example list says AI should not be used for 'recruitment, personnel, or disciplinary decision making', which keeps humans responsible for decisions about people (P73).
units.anchor: recruitment, personnel, or disciplinary decision making

units.why: The 4c example list includes 'creation of non-public instructional materials' as an output AI should not generate, a limit on instructor use of AI for teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: creation of non-public instructional materials
units.policy: AI tools should not be used to create non-public instructional materials.

units.why: The 4c example list ends with 'grading', so AI should not be used for grading; it limits AI in grading (nearest P46, humans assign grades).
units.anchor: non-public instructional materials; and grading.
units.policy: AI tools should not be used to generate outputs such as grading.
units.fit_note: Phrased as a 'should not' on grading as a non-public output, not an explicit statement that humans assign grades.

units.why: 4d: AI tools 'must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent, or violate any state or federal laws, or TTUHSC or TTU System policies', a general conduct ban (P74).
units.anchor: must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent

units.why: Additional guidance 5a warns that accepting click-through agreements 'may result in personal responsibility for compliance with the terms and conditions', a notice on contract terms and liability (P52 nearest: terms of use).
units.anchor: accepting click-through agreements without delegated signature authority may result in personal responsibility
units.frag_end: terms and conditions of the AI tool.
units.fit_note: About personal liability for terms of service, not copyright or ownership.

units.why: 5b: 'Contact TTUHSC IT before purchasing (or acquiring for free) AI tools', a procurement-review rule (P65).
units.anchor: Contact TTUHSC IT before purchasing (or acquiring for free) AI tools
units.frag_end: resources or data will be used.

units.why: 5c: 'Do not input Personal Information about TTUHSC employees, students, faculty, or other stakeholders into an AI tool' unless approved contracts exist; a privacy rule (P50).
units.anchor: Do not input Personal Information about TTUHSC employees, students, faculty

units.why: 5d: 'Users must adhere to the terms and conditions of AI tools and protect intellectual property rights', a licensing and copyright rule (P52).
units.anchor: Users must adhere to the terms and conditions of AI tools and protect intellectual property

units.why: 5d adds that library resources 'are subject to vendor licenses that may restrict AI use' and tells users to contact the Libraries; a limit on feeding licensed content to AI (P49 nearest).
units.anchor: Many digital resources provided by TTUHSC Libraries are subject to vendor licenses that may restrict
units.fit_note: Concerns licensed library content and vendor licenses, not course materials uploaded by students.

units.why: 5e: 'Always confirm the accuracy of AI-generated information before relying on it' since outputs 'may be inaccurate, biased, or fabricated'; this is verify-output (P31).
units.anchor: Always confirm the accuracy of AI-generated information before relying on it.

units.why: 5e: 'Users are responsible for any published content that incorporates AI-generated material' makes users answerable for what they publish (P29).
units.anchor: Users are responsible for any published content that incorporates AI-generated material.

units.why: 5f: 'Clearly disclose when written materials or other work products are generated with or derived from AI tools', a disclosure duty (P24).
units.anchor: Clearly disclose when written materials or other work products are generated with or derived from

units.why: 5f continues 'Transparency is required whenever AI outputs are used', extending the disclosure duty to any use of outputs (P24).
units.anchor: Transparency is required whenever AI outputs are used.

units.why: 5g: 'Do not present AI-generated outputs as your own' is a ban on passing off AI output as one's own work (P19).
units.anchor: Do not present AI-generated outputs as your own.
units.fit_note: Applies to all users and all work products, not only submitted student work.

units.why: 5g also says to 'ensure accuracy and avoid infringing on another party's intellectual property rights' when quoting or paraphrasing AI output, an IP rule (P52).
units.anchor: avoid infringing on another party’s intellectual property rights

units.why: 5h: 'Do not use AI tools to create malicious content, including malware' or bypass network security; a ban on malicious AI use (P74).
units.anchor: Do not use AI tools to create malicious content, including malware, viruses, worms, or trojan

notes: Single institutional operating policy; no school, computing or course documents. Mostly not coursework-specific. Several type assignments are partial fits (see fit_note).
